payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
Nik Kale wrote one of the most useful pieces on AI agent security to appear in May 2026. His premise is that the protections developed for the software supply chain — code signing, software bill of materials, SLSA provenance — were designed to verify that an artifact is what it claims to be. They were never built to verify how an artifact behaves after it ships.

For static code, that distinction rarely matters. For an AI tool whose behavior the calling agent has to trust at runtime, it matters constantly. A tool can have clean provenance and still poison the agent that selects it, because a description containing prompt-injection payloads passes every artifact check while corrupting the agent's selection logic. Or it can pass the initial verification and start returning different responses from the server weeks later. The signature is the same. The conduct is not.

His warning carries historical weight. He invokes the early-2000s HTTPS certificate problem as the closest analogue: the industry shipped strong identity guarantees back then and discovered, years later, that valid signatures could still be issued to phishing sites. Identity verified. Trust unestablished. Kale argues the agent-tool registry world risks repeating that mistake by leaning on SLSA provenance while behavior drifts underneath.

I want to use his piece to draw a line my own work has assumed but never spelled out. There are two kinds of provenance in active conversation right now. They are sometimes called the same name. They are not the same thing. Mistaking one for the other is how a research program gets dismissed by people who haven't read it closely.

Two regimes

The first kind is authorship provenance. It answers a question about origin. Who made this, when, and under what conditions? The verification happens once, at the moment of creation, and the result is bound to the artifact for the rest of its life. Cryptographic signatures at the DAW level. C2PA manifests embedded in the audio file. A claim about the human who made the work, carried through the distribution chain so platforms, rights holders, and listeners can read it later.

This is the regime my SSRN papers sit in. It is the regime the broader C2PA initiative sits in. It is the regime Digimarc's audio watermarking sits in. The thing being verified is identity at origin. The signal is one-shot.

The second kind is behavioral provenance. It answers a different question. Does this thing keep doing what it said it would do? The verification is continuous because the answer can change. A tool described as a calendar reader can be replaced server-side with a calendar exfiltrator. A model can be rebound to a different system prompt. An agent can drift after a few hundred steps. The thing being verified is conduct over time. The signal has to be live.

This is the regime Kale is writing in. It is the regime Invariant Labs occupies with the MCP Tool Poisoning Attack disclosure from April 2025. It is where OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications has been mapping the attack surface since December.

Why the names collapse

The word provenance does a lot of work in computer security. It came up in the SLSA framework, the SBOM movement, supply chain controls for code signing. All of those are origin claims. So when the AI agent security world started using the same vocabulary for the behavioral problem, the inherited assumption was that origin verification would translate. It does not. Origin verification is necessary. It is not the full answer for systems whose behavior is not fixed at the moment of release.

The cleanest way to see the difference is to ask what a successful attack looks like in each regime.

Against authorship provenance, the attack is impersonation. A human claims to have made something a different human made, or a machine claims human origin it does not have. The defense is cryptographic binding at creation. If you cannot produce the private key that signed the work at the moment it was created, your claim does not stand.

Against behavioral provenance, the attack is drift. A tool that passed verification yesterday returns different bytes today. A model that answered safely on launch begins to misroute requests three weeks in. The defense moves elsewhere. Runtime checks. Behavioral contracts. Allowlists on what tools can call what services. The kind of verification proxy Kale proposes between the agent and the tool, validating each invocation against the behavior the agent originally agreed to. Different problem. Different defense surface.

What this means for music

The trilogy I have been working through sits firmly in the first regime. The original paper proposed a cryptographic framework for human authorship verification in music distribution. The substrate paper went deeper on the infrastructure layer. The forthcoming third paper will extend the same regime into contributor identity and the long tail of independent creators. All three answer questions about origin.

That matters because the critique that almost always lands on provenance work in adjacent fields is some version of: provenance is not enough. The Kale piece makes that critique with precision in the agent-security context. The honest answer is that the critique is correct there and largely irrelevant here.

Music distribution does not have a behavioral drift problem in the agentic sense. A finished recording does not change its behavior server-side three weeks after release. The authorship claim, once bound to the work, does not need continuous re-verification of conduct. It needs a one-shot identity proof carried in the metadata. That is what the framework provides.

What music distribution does have, increasingly, is an attribution and royalty integrity problem. AI generated content polluting MLC matching. Sound-alike productions gaming algorithmic playlist placement. Catalog dilution at a scale no detection-first approach can keep up with. The argument for authorship provenance in this domain is not that it solves every adjacent question. The argument is that detection is structurally incapable of solving this one, and authorship provenance is the regime that addresses it directly.

Where the regimes meet

There is one place the two overlap, and it is worth flagging because the trilogy will eventually have to engage it. Music distribution increasingly involves agentic intermediaries. Rights management platforms. Royalty scanners. AI-assisted attribution tools that read provenance manifests and route payments accordingly. The moment those agents are reading authorship signals and taking action on them, the agent itself becomes part of the trust surface.

In that scenario, both regimes apply. The authorship claim has to be cryptographically sound. And the agent reading the claim has to be behaviorally trustworthy. A correctly signed manifest read by a poisoned agent is not a system that has solved attribution. It is a system with strong origin guarantees and a weak runtime substrate.

That is the kind of problem the next decade of music infrastructure will have to solve. It is not what any single paper or framework solves alone. But it is worth seeing clearly. Authorship provenance is a necessary condition for trustworthy music infrastructure. It is not a sufficient one. The trilogy makes the case for the necessary part. The sufficient part is downstream and requires the behavioral regime Kale's domain is building.

Two regimes. Different questions. Worth not collapsing them.
payload.title: Two kinds of provenance
